Since H is finite-dimensional, B is a finite-dimensional graded Hopf algebra: its multiplication m_B: B^i ⊗ B^j → B^{i+j} is the transpose of Δ: H^{i+j} → H^i ⊗ H^j (with the usual Koszul sign convention), its unit is ε, its counit is evaluation at 1, and its comultiplication is the transpose of m. As H is graded-cocommutative, B is graded-commutative: for b ∈ B^i, c ∈ B^j and x ∈ H^{i+j}, the H^i⊗H^j-component of Δ(x) satisfies ⟨bc, x⟩ = (-1)^{ij}⟨b⊗c, Δ(x)⟩, while graded cocommutativity of H gives ⟨c⊗b, Δ(x)⟩ = (-1)^{ij}⟨b⊗c, Δ(x)⟩, whence ⟨bc, x⟩ = (-1)^{ij}⟨cb, x⟩ and therefore bc = (-1)^{ij}cb. Also B^0 = (H^0)^* = k, dim_k B^1 = N, B^n = 0 for n > N, and dim_k B^N = 1.

Step 3 (indecomposables of B versus primitives of H). Let B^+ = ⊕_{n≥1} B^n and Q(B) = B^+/(B^+)^2, graded by Q(B)_n = B^n/(B^+B^+)^n for n ≥ 1 and Q(B)_0 = 0, where (B^+B^+)^n = Σ_{i+j=n, i,j≥1} B^iB^j. We claim that for every n ≥ 1 the annihilator of (B^+B^+)^n in H^n = (B^n)^* is exactly P_n.

Indeed, fix x ∈ H^n. For i,j ≥ 1 with i+j = n, the bilinear form B^i × B^j → k, (b,c) ↦ ⟨bc, x⟩, is, up to the sign (-1)^{ij} which is invertible in k, the pairing of b⊗c with the H^i⊗H^j-component of Δ(x) under the perfect pairings B^i × H^i → k and B^j × H^j → k. Hence ⟨bc, x⟩ = 0 for all b ∈ B^i and c ∈ B^j if and only if the H^i⊗H^j-component of Δ(x) vanishes. Therefore x annihilates (B^+B^+)^n if and only if Δ(x) has no component in H^i⊗H^j for any i,j ≥ 1 with i+j = n, i.e. if and only if Δ(x) ∈ H^0⊗H^n ⊕ H^n⊗H^0.

Since H^0 = k·1, write Δ(x) = 1⊗x_1 + x_2⊗1 with x_1, x_2 ∈ H^n. Applying ε⊗id gives x = (ε⊗id)Δ(x) = x_1, because ε(x_2) = 0 as n ≥ 1. Applying id⊗ε gives x = x_2. Thus Δ(x) = 1⊗x + x⊗1, i.e. x ∈ P_n. Conversely, if x ∈ P_n, then for b ∈ B^i, c ∈ B^j with i,j ≥ 1 we have ⟨bc, x⟩ = (-1)^{ij}⟨b⊗c, Δ(x)⟩ = (-1)^{ij}(ε(b)⟨c,x⟩ + ⟨b,x⟩ε(c)) = 0, since ε vanishes on positive-degree elements. Hence the annihilator is P_n, and the perfect pairing identifies (Q(B)_n)^* with P_n; in particular dim_k Q(B)_n = dim_k P_n. By Step 1, Q(B)_1 ≅ (H^1)^* has dimension N, and Q(B)_n = 0 for all n ≥ 2.

Step 4 (B is generated by B^1). For n ≥ 2 the equality Q(B)_n = 0 means B^n = (B^+B^+)^n = Σ_{i=1}^{n-1} B^iB^{n-i}. We prove by induction on n that B^n is spanned by the n-fold products b_1···b_n with b_j ∈ B^1. For n = 0 this is B^0 = k (the empty product), and for n = 1 it is trivial. For n ≥ 2, by induction each B^i (1 ≤ i ≤ n-1) is spanned by i-fold products of elements of B^1 and each B^{n-i} is spanned by (n-i)-fold products; hence each B^iB^{n-i} is spanned by n-fold products, and their sum B^n is spanned by n-fold products. Thus B is generated as a graded k-algebra by B^1.

Step 5 (upper bound). Since B^1 lies in odd degree 1, graded commutativity of B gives b_1···b_i b_{i+1}···b_n = -b_1···b_{i+1}b_i···b_n for all b_1,...,b_n ∈ B^1. Hence the n-fold multiplication map (B^1)^{⊗n} → B^n is alternating and therefore factors through the canonical surjection (B^1)^{⊗n} → ∧^n B^1, producing a linear map ∧^n B^1 → B^n. By Step 4 this map is surjective. Consequently dim_k B^n ≤ dim_k ∧^n B^1 = binom(N,n), with the convention binom(N,n) = 0 for n > N.

Step 6 (lower bound). By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_exterior_subalgebra_injects, the multiplication map ∧^n H^1 → H^n is injective for every n ≥ 0. Hence dim_k H^n ≥ dim_k ∧^n H^1 = binom(N,n).

Step 7 (conclusion). Since B^n = (H^n)^*, we have dim_k B^n = dim_k H^n. Combining Steps 5 and 6 gives binom(N,n) ≤ dim_k H^n = dim_k B^n ≤ binom(N,n), so dim_k H^n = binom(N,n). The injective linear map ∧^n H^1 → H^n therefore goes between finite-dimensional k-vector spaces of the same dimension, hence is an isomorphism. This holds for every n ≥ 0. (For N = 0 the same argument applies; explicitly H^1 = 0, H^n = 0 for n > 0, and the maps are the identity on k in degree 0 and zero maps between zero spaces in positive degrees.) ∎

statement: Let \(k\) be a field, let \(M\ge1\) be an integer, let \(C_1,\dots,C_M\) be smooth projective geometrically connected curves over \(k\), and let \(Z\subset C_1\times_k\cdots\times_k C_M\) be a closed subscheme of pure dimension \(n\) with \(0\le n\le M\). Then for every irreducible component \(W\) of \(Z\) there exist indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_n\le M\), the index set being empty when \(n=0\) and \(\operatorname{pr}_{i_1,\dots,i_n}\) then being the structure morphism to \(\operatorname{Spec}k\), such that the restriction of \(\operatorname{pr}_{i_1,\dots,i_n}\) to \(W\) is dominant onto its image and the induced extension of function fields is finite.
proof:
Proof. We prove the statement as written, with the indices allowed to depend on the irreducible component \(W\). If \(Z\) has no irreducible component, the assertion is vacuous. Assume \(Z\) is nonempty and put \(P=C_1\times_k\cdots\times_k C_M\). Fix an irreducible component \(W\) of \(Z\) and give it the reduced induced closed subscheme structure. Then \(W\) is integral and, since \(Z\) is pure of dimension \(n\), we have \(\dim W=n\).

We use the standard dimension theorem: if \(X\) is an integral scheme of finite type over a field \(k\), then \(\dim X=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(X)\). For completeness, here is a proof. Choose a nonempty affine open \(\operatorname{Spec} A\subset X\). Then \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-domain with fraction field \(\kappa(X)\). By Noether normalization there exist algebraically independent elements \(y_1,\dots,y_d\in A\) over \(k\) such that \(A\) is finite as a module over \(k[y_1,\dots,y_d]\). Finite ring extensions preserve Krull dimension, so \(\dim A=d\), and \(d=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(X)\). Since \(X\) is integral, every nonempty open subscheme has the same dimension as \(X\), so \(\dim X=\dim A=d\).

For each \(i\), let \(x_i=\operatorname{pr}_i(\eta_W)\) be the image of the generic point of \(W\) in \(C_i\). Choose a nonempty affine open \(U_i\subset C_i\) containing \(x_i\), and put \(A_i=\mathcal O_{C_i}(U_i)\). Since \(C_i\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve, it is an integral scheme of finite type over \(k\) of dimension \(1\); hence \(A_i\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-domain of dimension \(1\). Let \(U=\prod_i U_i=\operatorname{Spec} A\), where \(A=A_1\otimes_k\cdots\otimes_k A_M\). Because \(\eta_W\) lies in \(U\), the open subscheme \(W\cap U\) is nonempty and dense in \(W\); it is integral and corresponds to a prime ideal \(\mathfrak p\subset A\). Put \(B=A/\mathfrak p\), so \(B\) is a domain with fraction field \(\kappa(W)\). For each \(i\), let \(B_i\) be the image of \(A_i\) in \(B\) and \(L_i=\operatorname{Frac}(B_i)\subset\kappa(W)\). Since \(B_i\) is a quotient of \(A_i\), it is a finitely generated \(k\)-domain of dimension at most \(1\); by the dimension theorem, \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k L_i=\dim B_i\le1\). The images of the \(A_i\) generate \(B\) as a \(k\)-algebra, hence the fields \(L_i\) generate \(\kappa(W)\) as a field over \(k\).

Since \(\kappa(W)\) is finitely generated over \(k\) and is generated by \(\bigcup_i L_i\), choose a finite subset \(T\subset\bigcup_i L_i\) which generates \(\kappa(W)\) as a field. Let \(S\) be a maximal algebraically independent subset of \(T\). Then \(S\) is a transcendence basis of \(\kappa(W)/k\): every \(t\in T\) is algebraic over \(k(S)\) by maximality, so \(\kappa(W)\) is algebraic over \(k(S)\). Therefore \(|S|=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(W)=\dim W=n\), by the dimension theorem and \(\dim W=n\). If \(S\) contained two distinct elements \(a,b\) of the same \(L_i\), then \(a,b\) would be algebraically independent over \(k\), so \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k L_i\ge2\), contradiction. Thus \(S\) contains at most one element from each \(L_i\). For each \(s\in S\), choose an index \(i(s)\) with \(s\in L_{i(s)}\). If \(s\ne t\) and \(i(s)=i(t)\), then both \(s\) and \(t\) lie in \(L_{i(s)}\), impossible; hence the indices \(i(s)\) are distinct. Sorting them gives \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_n\le M\) (the list is empty when \(n=0\)), and \(S\subset\bigcup_{j=1}^n L_{i_j}\).

Let \(P_I=\prod_{j=1}^n C_{i_j}\) (with \(P_I=\operatorname{Spec} k\) when \(n=0\)), and let \(\pi_I:P\to P_I\) be the projection. Let \(Y\subset P_I\) be the reduced closed subscheme whose underlying topological space is the closure of \(\pi_I(W)\). Then \(Y\) is integral and \(f=\pi_I|_W:W\to Y\) is dominant. We claim that \(\kappa(Y)\) is the compositum of the fields \(L_{i_j}\) inside \(\kappa(W)\). Indeed, over \(U_I=\prod_j U_{i_j}=\operatorname{Spec} A_I\) with \(A_I=\bigotimes_j A_{i_j}\), the morphism \(W\cap U\to U_I\) corresponds to the natural map \(A_I\to B\). Its scheme-theoretic image is \(\operatorname{Spec}(A_I/J)\), where \(J=\ker(A_I\to B)\), whose function field is the subfield of \(\kappa(W)\) generated by the images of the \(A_{i_j}\), i.e. the compositum of the \(L_{i_j}\). Passing to the closure in \(P_I\) does not change the function field, since \(Y\cap U_I\) is dense in \(Y\). Thus the claim holds. In particular, \(k(S)\subset\kappa(Y)\).

By the dimension theorem, \(\dim Y=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Y)\). Since \(\kappa(Y)\subset\kappa(W)\), we have \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Y)\le\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(W)=n\). Since \(k(S)\subset\kappa(Y)\) and \(|S|=n\), we have \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Y)\ge n\). Hence \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Y)=n\) and \(\dim Y=n\). We also have \(\dim W=n\), so \(f:W\to Y\) is a dominant morphism of integral varieties of the same dimension \(n\).

Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_generic_fiber_integral to \(f:W\to Y\), taking its \(X\) to be our \(W\) and its integral closed subscheme to be the whole of \(X\). It says that the generic fibre \(W_\eta=W\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(Y)\) is integral of dimension \(\dim W-\dim Y=0\) and, since \(\dim W=\dim Y\), is the spectrum of a finite field extension of \(\kappa(Y)\) of degree \([\kappa(W):\kappa(Y)]\). Therefore \(\kappa(W)/\kappa(Y)\) is finite. Thus the restriction of \(\pi_I\) to \(W\) is dominant onto its image \(Y\) and induces a finite extension of function fields. Since \(W\) was an arbitrary irreducible component of \(Z\), the lemma follows.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let ⟨−,−⟩: V×V→K be a perfect bilinear form, and let T∈GL_K(V) satisfy ⟨Tx,Ty⟩=⟨x,y⟩ for all x,y∈V. Put N=T−id_V. If N^2=0 and rank N=1, then there exist a nonzero δ∈V and c∈K^× such that N(x)=c⟨x,δ⟩δ for all x∈V and ⟨δ,δ⟩=0.
proof:
Write the bilinear form as B(x,y)=⟨x,y⟩. Since N^2=0, we have T=id_V+N and (id_V+N)(id_V−N)=id_V−N^2=id_V, so T^{-1}=id_V−N. Both T and T^{-1} are isometries of the form.

For arbitrary x,y∈V, the isometry identity for T gives
0=⟨Tx,Ty⟩−⟨x,y⟩=⟨x+Nx,y+Ny⟩−⟨x,y⟩=⟨Nx,y⟩+⟨x,Ny⟩+⟨Nx,Ny⟩.  (1)
Similarly, the isometry identity for T^{-1} gives
0=⟨T^{-1}x,T^{-1}y⟩−⟨x,y⟩=⟨x−Nx,y−Ny⟩−⟨x,y⟩=−⟨Nx,y⟩−⟨x,Ny⟩+⟨Nx,Ny⟩.  (2)
Adding (1) and (2) yields 2⟨Nx,Ny⟩=0. Since char K=0, 2 is invertible, hence
⟨Nx,Ny⟩=0 for all x,y∈V.
Substituting this into (1) gives
⟨Nx,y⟩+⟨x,Ny⟩=0, i.e. ⟨Nx,y⟩=−⟨x,Ny⟩ for all x,y∈V.  (3)

Because rank N=1, the image of N is a one-dimensional subspace of V. Choose a nonzero vector δ spanning im N. Then there is a linear functional φ:V→K such that
N(x)=φ(x)δ for all x∈V.
Since N has rank 1, N≠0, so φ≠0. From N^2=0 we get, for every x∈V,
0=N^2(x)=N(φ(x)δ)=φ(x)N(δ)=φ(x)φ(δ)δ.
Choosing x with φ(x)≠0 and using δ≠0 gives φ(δ)=0. Thus N(δ)=φ(δ)δ=0.

Now put y=δ in (3). Since N(δ)=0, we obtain
0=⟨Nx,δ⟩=⟨φ(x)δ,δ⟩=φ(x)⟨δ,δ⟩
for every x∈V. Because φ≠0, choose x with φ(x)≠0; then ⟨δ,δ⟩=0.

Finally, using N(x)=φ(x)δ and N(y)=φ(y)δ in (3), we get
φ(x)⟨δ,y⟩=−φ(y)⟨x,δ⟩ for all x,y∈V.  (4)
Since the form is perfect and δ≠0, the linear functional y↦⟨δ,y⟩ is not identically zero; otherwise δ would lie in the radical of the form. Hence there exists y_0∈V with ⟨δ,y_0⟩≠0. Taking y=y_0 in (4) gives
φ(x)⟨δ,y_0⟩=−φ(y_0)⟨x,δ⟩,
so
φ(x)=c⟨x,δ⟩, where c=−φ(y_0)/⟨δ,y_0⟩.
If c were 0, then φ would be the zero functional, contradicting φ≠0. Therefore c∈K^×. Consequently,
N(x)=φ(x)δ=c⟨x,δ⟩δ for all x∈V,
and we have already shown ⟨δ,δ⟩=0. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, and put k=F̄_q. Let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_q. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ℓ(1) and use it to identify Tate twists with Q_ℓ. Let H be an F_q-rational very ample divisor on S with cycle class ξ∈H²_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ), let L be cup product with ξ, put P²=ker(L:H²_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ)→H⁴_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ)), and let β(x,y)=tr_S(x∪y) for x,y∈H²_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ), where tr_S:H⁴_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ)→Q_ℓ is the Poincaré duality trace normalized by tr_S(cl(z))=[κ(z):F_q] for closed points z of S. Let W be the Q-linear span of the cycle classes of the F_q-rational divisors D on S with cl(D)∈P², and suppose that P²=W⊗_Q Q_ℓ. Then for every field embedding σ:Q̄_ℓ↪C, the Hermitian form h_σ on W⊗_{Q,σ}C defined by h_σ(x⊗a,y⊗b)=a·conj(b)·β(x,y) is negative definite.
proof:
Let \(H^2=H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^4=H^4_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Since \(S\) is smooth projective over \(k\) and \(\ell\neq p\), these are finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces, and \(\operatorname{tr}_S\colon H^4\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) is the Poincaré duality trace normalized as in the statement.

**Step 0 (bilinearity and symmetry of \(\beta\)).** The cup product is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear and \(\operatorname{tr}_S\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear, hence \(\beta\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear. For \(x,y\in H^2\), graded commutativity of the cup product gives \(x\cup y=(-1)^{2\cdot 2}y\cup x=y\cup x\), so \(\beta(x,y)=\beta(y,x)\). Thus \(\beta\) is a symmetric \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear form on \(H^2\).

**Step 1 (\(W\subseteq P^2\) and its generators).** The map \(L\colon H^2\to H^4\), \(x\mapsto x\cup\xi\), is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear, so \(P^2=\ker L\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspace of \(H^2\). By definition \(W\) is the \(\mathbb Q\)-linear span of the classes \(\operatorname{cl}(D)\in P^2\) of \(F_q\)-rational divisors \(D\); since \(P^2\) is closed under addition and under multiplication by \(\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb Q_\ell\), we have \(W\subseteq P^2\). Every element \(x\in W\) is, by definition, a finite \(\mathbb Q\)-linear combination \(x=\sum_i q_i\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\) with \(q_i\in\mathbb Q\) and \(D_i\) \(F_q\)-rational divisors such that \(\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\in P^2\). Since \(S\) is smooth, each divisor \(D_i\) is a Cartier divisor.

**Step 2 (negative values and rationality on \(W\)).** Let \(x\in W\setminus\{0\}\). Then \(x\in P^2\) by Step 1, and \(x\) is a nonzero \(\mathbb Q\)-linear combination of cycle classes of \(F_q\)-rational Cartier divisors. Applying Miner/16d24b0281973336/d3e72a with \(m=1\) (so \(F_{q^m}=F_q\)) to the surface \(S\), the very ample divisor \(H\), the class \(\xi\), the map \(L\), the space \(P^2\), the trace \(\operatorname{tr}_S\), and the form \(\beta\), we obtain
\[
\beta(x,x)\in\mathbb Q_{<0}. \tag{2.1}
\]
Now let \(x,y\in W\). If \(x+y\neq0\), then by (2.1) \(\beta(x+y,x+y)\in\mathbb Q\), and also \(\beta(x,x)\in\mathbb Q\) and \(\beta(y,y)\in\mathbb Q\) (with the convention \(\beta(0,0)=0\)). Hence
\[
2\beta(x,y)=\beta(x+y,x+y)-\beta(x,x)-\beta(y,y)\in\mathbb Q,
\]
so \(\beta(x,y)\in\mathbb Q\). If \(x+y=0\), then \(\beta(x,y)=-\beta(x,x)\in\mathbb Q\). Therefore
\[
\beta(W,W)\subseteq\mathbb Q. \tag{2.2}
\]

**Step 3 (well-definedness and Hermitian symmetry of \(h_\sigma\)).** Let \(\sigma\colon\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) be a field embedding. Since \(\operatorname{char}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=0\), the restriction \(\sigma|_{\mathbb Q}\colon\mathbb Q\to\mathbb C\) is a field homomorphism, hence \(\sigma(q)=q\) for every \(q\in\mathbb Q\). By (2.2), \(\sigma(\beta(x,y))=\beta(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in W\). Also, since \(\sigma|_{\mathbb Q}=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb Q}\), the tensor product \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q,\sigma}\mathbb C\) is the ordinary tensor product \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\).

Define \(h_\sigma\) on elementary tensors by
\[
h_\sigma(x\otimes a,y\otimes b)=a\,\overline{b}\,\beta(x,y),\qquad x,y\in W,\ a,b\in\mathbb C.
\]
We check that this is well defined on the balanced tensor product. For \(\lambda\in\mathbb Q\), in the first variable \((\lambda x)\otimes a=x\otimes(\sigma(\lambda)a)=x\otimes(\lambda a)\), and
\[
h_\sigma(\lambda x\otimes a,y\otimes b)=a\overline{b}\beta(\lambda x,y)=\lambda a\overline{b}\beta(x,y)=h_\sigma(x\otimes\lambda a,y\otimes b).
\]
In the second variable \((\lambda y)\otimes b=y\otimes(\lambda b)\), and
\[
h_\sigma(x\otimes a,\lambda y\otimes b)=a\overline{b}\beta(x,\lambda y)=\lambda a\overline{b}\beta(x,y)=a\overline{\lambda b}\beta(x,y)=h_\sigma(x\otimes a,y\otimes\lambda b),
\]
where we used \(\overline{\lambda}=\lambda\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb R\). Additivity in each variable follows from the bilinearity of \(\beta\). Hence \(h_\sigma\) is well defined. It is \(\mathbb C\)-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second, and
\[
h_\sigma(y\otimes b,x\otimes a)=b\overline{a}\beta(y,x)=\overline{a\overline{b}\beta(x,y)}=\overline{h_\sigma(x\otimes a,y\otimes b)},
\]
because \(\beta(y,x)=\beta(x,y)\in\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb R\). Thus \(h_\sigma\) is a Hermitian form on \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q,\sigma}\mathbb C\).

**Step 4 (negative definiteness of \(h_\sigma\)).** If \(W=0\), the assertion is vacuous. Assume \(W\neq0\). By the hypothesis \(P^2=W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ell\) and the flatness of \(\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q_\ell\), the natural map \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ell\to H^2\) is injective with image \(P^2\), so \(\dim_{\mathbb Q}W=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}P^2<\infty\). Put \(m=\dim_{\mathbb Q}W\ge1\) and choose a \(\mathbb Q\)-basis \(x_1,\dots,x_m\) of \(W\). Let
\[
B=(\beta(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^m\in M_m(\mathbb Q),
\]
which is symmetric by Step 0 and rational by (2.2).

For every \(c=(c_1,\dots,c_m)^T\in\mathbb Q^m\setminus\{0\}\), the element \(\sum_i c_i x_i\in W\) is nonzero because \(x_1,\dots,x_m\) is a basis, so by (2.1)
\[
c^TBc=\beta\Big(\sum_i c_i x_i,\sum_j c_j x_j\Big)<0. \tag{4.1}
\]
In particular \(B\) is negative definite over \(\mathbb Q\), hence nondegenerate: if \(Bc=0\) with \(c\in\mathbb Q^m\), then \(c^TBc=0\), so \(c=0\) by (4.1).

We now diagonalize \(B\) by symmetric Gram–Schmidt over \(\mathbb Q\). We construct a \(\mathbb Q\)-basis \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) of \(\mathbb Q^m\) with
\[
v_i^TBv_j=0\quad(i\neq j),\qquad v_i^TBv_i=-d_i,\quad d_i\in\mathbb Q_{>0}.
\]
Inductively, suppose \(v_1,\dots,v_k\) (\(k<m\)) have been constructed with the stated orthogonality. Let
\[
U_k=\{c\in\mathbb Q^m: v_i^TBc=0\text{ for }i=1,\dots,k\}.
\]
Each functional \(c\mapsto v_i^TBc\) is nonzero because \(B\) is nondegenerate and \(v_i\neq0\); hence \(U_k\) is the intersection of \(k\) proper hyperplanes in \(\mathbb Q^m\), so \(\dim_{\mathbb Q}U_k\ge m-k>0\). Choose \(v_{k+1}\in U_k\setminus\{0\}\). Then \(v_{k+1}^TBv_{k+1}<0\) by (4.1), so \(d_{k+1}:=-v_{k+1}^TBv_{k+1}\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). Moreover \(v_{k+1}\notin\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\): otherwise \(v_{k+1}=\sum_{i\le k}a_iv_i\) and then \(v_{k+1}^TBv_{k+1}=\sum_i a_i(v_i^TBv_{k+1})=0\), a contradiction. Thus \(v_1,\dots,v_{k+1}\) are \(\mathbb Q\)-linearly independent. After \(m\) steps we obtain a \(\mathbb Q\)-basis.

Let \(P\in GL_m(\mathbb Q)\) be the matrix whose columns are \(v_1,\dots,v_m\). Then
\[
P^TBP=D:=\operatorname{diag}(-d_1,\dots,-d_m),\qquad d_i\in\mathbb Q_{>0},
\]
equivalently
\[
B=P^{-T}DP^{-1}. \tag{4.2}
\]

Now let \(v=\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\otimes a_i\in W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\) be nonzero, with \(a_i\in\mathbb C\). Since \(x_1,\dots,x_m\) is a \(\mathbb Q\)-basis of \(W\), the elements \(x_i\otimes1\) form a \(\mathbb C\)-basis of \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\); hence \(a=(a_1,\dots,a_m)^T\neq0\). Using (4.2) and the symmetry of \(B\),
\[
h_\sigma(v,v)=\sum_{i,j}a_i\overline{a_j}\beta(x_i,x_j)=a^*Ba=a^*P^{-T}DP^{-1}a.
\]
Put \(b=P^{-1}a\in\mathbb C^m\); then \(b\neq0\) because \(P\) is invertible and \(a\neq0\), and
\[
h_\sigma(v,v)=b^*Db=-\sum_{i=1}^m d_i|b_i|^2<0,
\]
because every \(d_i\) is a positive real number and \(b\neq0\). Hence \(h_\sigma\) is negative definite.

**Remark on the corrected linear algebra.** The previous attempt claimed that from (4.1) one can find \(P\in GL_m(\mathbb Q)\) with \(P^TBP=-I_m\), equivalently \(B=-N^TN\) with \(N\in GL_m(\mathbb Q)\). This is false: for example \(B=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-9\end{pmatrix}\) is negative definite over \(\mathbb Q\) (its leading principal minors are \(-2<0\) and \(\det B=17>0\)), but \(\det B=17\) is not a square in \(\mathbb Q\), whereas \(\det(-N^TN)=\det(N)^2\) would be. The correct conclusion of symmetric Gram–Schmidt over \(\mathbb Q\) is \(P^TBP=\operatorname{diag}(-d_1,\dots,-d_m)\) with \(d_i\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\), which is exactly what is proved above and is sufficient, since the \(d_i\) are positive real numbers and hence \(-\sum_i d_i|b_i|^2<0\) for \(b\neq0\). No rational factorization \(B=-N^TN\) is needed or asserted.

This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(d\ge1\) and let \(X\subset\mathbb P^{d+1}_{\mathbb F_q}\) be a smooth geometrically connected hypersurface of pure dimension \(d\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), and let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(\mathcal O_X(1)\). Then for every integer \(n\) with \(0\le n<d\), the space \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) equals \(\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot\xi^{n/2}\) if \(n\) is even and is zero if \(n\) is odd.
proof:
Let \(P=\mathbb{P}^{d+1}_{\mathbb{F}_q}\), let \(i:X\hookrightarrow P\) be the closed immersion, and let \(j:U=P\setminus X\hookrightarrow P\) be the complementary open immersion. Put \(k=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q\).

First, \(X\) is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor on \(P\). Indeed, as a hypersurface it is the zero scheme of a nonzero homogeneous form of some degree \(e\ge1\), so \(\mathcal{O}_P(X)\cong\mathcal{O}_P(e)\), which is ample because \(\mathcal{O}_P(1)\) is ample and \(e>0\). Also \(\dim X=d<d+1=\dim P\), so \(X\subsetneq P\) and \(X\neq\emptyset\). By hypothesis \(X\) is smooth of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). The ambient \(P\) is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(D=d+1\ge2\). Therefore lemma_hc_vanishing_ample_complement, applied to \(P\) and its divisor \(X\), gives
\[
H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=0 \quad\text{for every } m<d+1. \tag{1}
\]

By lemma_localization_les_finite_type applied to the pair \((P_k,X_k)\), there is a long exact sequence
\[
\cdots\to H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\to H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\xrightarrow{i^*} H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\to H^{m+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\to\cdots. \tag{2}
\]
For any integer \(n\) with \(0\le n<d\), we have \(n<d+1\) and \(n+1\le d<d+1\), so (1) gives \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=H^{n+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=0\). Exactness of (2) then shows that
\[
i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim} H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \tag{3}
\]
is an isomorphism.

Let \(h=c_1(\mathcal{O}_P(1))\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\). By lemma_201, with projective space \(P_k=\mathbb{P}^{d+1}_k\), the graded \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-algebra \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\) is \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell[h]/(h^{d+2})\). Thus for every \(m\ge0\),
\[
H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=\mathbb{Q}_\ell\, h^{m/2} \text{ if } m \text{ is even},\quad\text{and}\quad H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=0 \text{ if } m \text{ is odd}, \tag{4}
\]
with \(h^i\neq0\) for \(0\le i\le d+1\). In particular, for \(n<d\), the space \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\) is one-dimensional generated by \(h^{n/2}\) if \(n\) is even, and is zero if \(n\) is odd.

Let \(\xi=\operatorname{cl}(\mathcal{O}_X(1))\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\). Since \(\mathcal{O}_X(1)=i^*\mathcal{O}_P(1)\), functoriality of cycle classes (equivalently, of first Chern classes) gives
\[
\xi=i^*h. \tag{5}
\]
For completeness, here is a justification of (5). The cycle class of a line bundle is its first Chern class. For each \(r\ge1\), the Kummer sequence \(0\to\mu_{\ell^r}\to\mathbb{G}_m\xrightarrow{\ell^r}\mathbb{G}_m\to0\) on \(P_k\) and on \(X_k\) is functorial in the morphism \(i\); naturality of the associated long exact sequences gives \(\delta_X(i^*L)=i^*\delta_P(L)\) for every line bundle \(L\) on \(P_k\), where \(\delta\) is the connecting homomorphism \(\operatorname{Pic}\to H^2(\mu_{\ell^r})\). Passing to the inverse limit over \(r\) and tensoring with \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\) yields \(c_1(i^*L)=i^*c_1(L)\). Taking \(L=\mathcal{O}_P(1)\) gives (5). (The Kummer sequence and its functoriality are recorded in lemma_kummer_h1.)

Now combine (3), (4), (5). If \(n<d\) is odd, then \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=0\), hence by (3) \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=0\). If \(n<d\) is even, then \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=\mathbb{Q}_\ell h^{n/2}\), and (3) and (5) give
\[
H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)
=i^*\bigl(\mathbb{Q}_\ell h^{n/2}\bigr)
=\mathbb{Q}_\ell (i^*h)^{n/2}
=\mathbb{Q}_\ell \xi^{n/2}.
\]
For \(n=0\), \(h^0=\xi^0=1\). This proves the lemma.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(M\ge1\), let \(C_1,\dots,C_M\) be smooth projective geometrically connected curves over \(\mathbb F_q\), put \(Y=C_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}C_M\), and let \(G\) be a finite group of order prime to \(\ell\) acting on \(Y\) by \(\mathbb F_q\)-automorphisms such that the quotient \(X=Y/G\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\). Then the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\), and its scalar extension to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable.
proof:
Proof. Put k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q and let \sigma: k\to k, \sigma(c)=c^q, be the q-power Frobenius field automorphism. For a scheme Z of finite type over \mathbb F_q write Z_k = Z\times_{\mathbb F_q} k and F_Z = (\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times \mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*. By lemma_6a, for every n \ge 0 the map F_Z is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). We must prove that F_X is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge0 and that F_X\otimes \mathrm{id}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} is diagonalizable on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.

Step 1 (Y is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over \mathbb F_q). By hypothesis each C_i is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over \mathbb F_q. A fibre product over a field of smooth (resp. projective) schemes is smooth (resp. projective), so Y = C_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}C_M is smooth and projective over \mathbb F_q. For geometric connectedness, Y_k = (C_1)_k\times_k\cdots\times_k(C_M)_k and each (C_i)_k is connected. Claim: if K is an algebraically closed field and A, B are connected K-schemes of finite type, then A\times_K B is connected. Indeed, every closed point of a K-scheme of finite type has residue field a finite extension of K (Zariski's lemma), hence equal to K because K is algebraically closed; so A(K) and B(K) are nonempty, and they are dense in A and B respectively (every nonempty open subset of A contains a closed point, i.e. a K-point). Choose b_0\in B(K). For each a\in A(K) the set S_a := (\{a\}\times B)\cup (A\times\{b_0\}) is a union of two connected sets ({a}\times B\cong B and A\times\{b_0\}\cong A) meeting in the point (a,b_0), hence is connected. All the S_a contain the connected set A\times\{b_0\}, so U := \bigcup_{a\in A(K)} S_a = (A(K)\times B)\cup (A\times\{b_0\}) is connected. Moreover A(K)\times B is dense in A\times_K B: the projection A\times_K B\to A is flat and locally of finite presentation, hence open, so every nonempty open subset of A\times_K B has an image in A that is nonempty open and therefore meets A(K). Thus U is dense in A\times_K B; the closure of a connected set is connected, so A\times_K B = \overline U is connected. Applying this claim iteratively to (C_1)_k,\dots,(C_M)_k gives that Y_k is connected, i.e. Y is geometrically connected over \mathbb F_q. Also \dim Y = M.

Step 2 (semisimplicity on Y). Apply lemma_341 with its m equal to our M and its product X equal to our Y: the q-power arithmetic Frobenius F_Y acts semisimply on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every integer n\ge0.

Step 3 (semisimplicity on X). By hypothesis G is a finite group of \mathbb F_q-automorphisms of Y whose order is prime to \ell, and the quotient X = Y/G is smooth projective and geometrically connected over \mathbb F_q. Step 1 verifies the remaining hypothesis of lemma_283 (with its Y equal to our Y and its X equal to our X), and Step 2 supplies its assumption. Hence lemma_283 gives: F_X = (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^* is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every integer n\ge0. This is the first assertion of the lemma.

Step 4 (finite-dimensionality). X is smooth projective, hence proper, over \mathbb F_q. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob to X and to the constant constructible complex K = \mathbb Q_\ell\in D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, we get that V_n := H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space for every n. By lemma_6a the operator T_n := F_X|_{V_n} lies in \mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_n).

Step 5 (diagonalizability of the scalar extension). Fix n\ge0 and put V = V_n, T = T_n. By Step 3, T is semisimple over \mathbb Q_\ell, i.e. its minimal polynomial \mu_T\in\mathbb Q_\ell[x] is squarefree. By lemma_64(iii) applied with k = \mathbb Q_\ell and K = \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell (a field extension of characteristic 0), the operator T\otimes\mathrm{id} on V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is again semisimple. Concretely, \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell[T]\cong \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[x]/(\mu_T) embeds into \mathrm{End}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell), so the minimal polynomial of T\otimes\mathrm{id} is \mu_T viewed in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[x], and \mu_T stays squarefree there because a Bezout relation \mu_T g+\mu_T' h = 1 in \mathbb Q_\ell[x] persists after extending scalars.

We use the following elementary fact: if K is an algebraically closed field, W a finite-dimensional K-vector space and S\in\mathrm{End}_K(W), then S is semisimple (minimal polynomial squarefree) if and only if S is diagonalizable. Proof: if W has a basis of eigenvectors with pairwise distinct eigenvalues \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r, then \mu_S = \prod_{j=1}^r (x-\lambda_j) is squarefree. Conversely, if \mu_S is squarefree, then, K being algebraically closed, \mu_S = \prod_{j=1}^r (x-\lambda_j) with the \lambda_j pairwise distinct; by the Chinese remainder theorem K[x]/(\mu_S)\cong\prod_{j=1}^r K[x]/(x-\lambda_j)\cong K^r, and since \mu_S(S)=0 the K[x]-module W is a module over K[x]/(\mu_S); the standard idempotents e_j\in K[x]/(\mu_S) corresponding to the factors give W = \bigoplus_{j=1}^r e_jW = \bigoplus_{j=1}^r \ker(S-\lambda_j), so W is spanned by eigenvectors of S.

Applying this fact with K = \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, W = V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell and S = T\otimes\mathrm{id} shows that F_X\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} is diagonalizable on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. Since n\ge0 was arbitrary, both assertions of the lemma are proved.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(f:S\to C\) be a surjective morphism over \(\mathbb F_q\) such that \(f^*:H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism. Let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of an \(\mathbb F_q\)-rational very ample divisor on \(S\). Then the map \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^3_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(x\mapsto x\cup\xi\), is an isomorphism.
proof:
Notation. Put H^n(S) := H^n_ét(S_k, Q_ℓ) and H^n(C) := H^n_ét(C_k, Q_ℓ). Fix once and for all the nonzero element u_0 ∈ Q_ℓ(1) given in the statement and identify Q_ℓ(n) with Q_ℓ by u_0^n ↦ 1; in particular Q_ℓ(-1) and Q_ℓ(-2) are identified with Q_ℓ. For a smooth projective geometrically connected variety Z of pure dimension d over F_q let tr_Z : H^{2d}(Z) → Q_ℓ be the trace isomorphism of lemma_77(a) (with m = 1), normalized by tr_Z(cl(w)) = [κ(w) : F_q] for every closed point w of Z; composed with the above identification this is a Q_ℓ-linear isomorphism onto Q_ℓ. Note that then tr_Z(cl(w)) ≠ 0 for every closed point w, since [κ(w) : F_q] is a positive integer and Q ⊂ Q_ℓ.

Step 1: the two Poincaré dualities. By lemma_77(b) applied to the surface S with d = 2 and n = 1, the pairing
  ⟨ , ⟩_S : H^1(S) × H^3(S) → Q_ℓ(-2) ≅ Q_ℓ,  ⟨x, z⟩_S := tr_S(x ∪ z),
is a perfect pairing of Q_ℓ-vector spaces. By lemma_77(b) applied to the curve C with d = 1 and n = 1, the pairing
  ⟨ , ⟩_C : H^1(C) × H^1(C) → Q_ℓ(-1) ≅ Q_ℓ,  ⟨u, v⟩_C := tr_C(u ∪ v),
is a perfect pairing of Q_ℓ-vector spaces. Also, by lemma_77(a) with d = 2 (resp. d = 1), tr_S : H^4(S) → Q_ℓ and tr_C : H^2(C) → Q_ℓ are isomorphisms, so H^4(S) and H^2(C) are one-dimensional over Q_ℓ.

Step 2: a bilinear form β on H^1(S) and its relation to the map L. Define
  β : H^1(S) × H^1(S) → Q_ℓ,  β(x, y) := tr_S(x ∪ ξ ∪ y),
and let L : H^1(S) → H^3(S), L(y) := y ∪ ξ, be the map appearing in the statement. Since x, y have degree 1 and ξ has degree 2, graded commutativity of the cup product (α ∪ β' = (-1)^{deg α · deg β'} β' ∪ α) gives
  x ∪ ξ ∪ y = (x ∪ ξ) ∪ y = ((-1)^{1·2} ξ ∪ x) ∪ y = ξ ∪ x ∪ y,
  x ∪ (y ∪ ξ) = x ∪ ((-1)^{2·1} ξ ∪ y) = x ∪ ξ ∪ y = ξ ∪ x ∪ y,
so x ∪ ξ ∪ y = x ∪ (y ∪ ξ) = x ∪ L(y). Hence
  β(x, y) = tr_S(x ∪ L(y)) = ⟨x, L(y)⟩_S   for all x, y ∈ H^1(S).   (2.1)
Let ψ : H^3(S) → H^1(S)^* be the Q_ℓ-linear map ψ(z) := ⟨ · , z⟩_S, where H^1(S)^* is the Q_ℓ-dual; ψ is an isomorphism because ⟨ , ⟩_S is perfect. Let φ : H^1(S) → H^1(S)^* be φ(y) := β( · , y). By (2.1), φ = ψ ∘ L. Consequently
  L is an isomorphism  ⟺  φ is an isomorphism.   (2.2)
Indeed, if L is an isomorphism then φ = ψ ∘ L is a composite of isomorphisms; conversely, if φ is an isomorphism then L = ψ^{-1} ∘ φ is a composite of isomorphisms. Thus it suffices to prove that β is a perfect pairing, i.e. that φ is an isomorphism.

Step 3: computing β on the image of f^*. Since by hypothesis f^* : H^1(C) → H^1(S) is an isomorphism, every x ∈ H^1(S) is of the form x = f^*u for a unique u ∈ H^1(C), and every y ∈ H^1(S) is of the form y = f^*v for a unique v ∈ H^1(C). Pullback f^* is a homomorphism of graded Q_ℓ-algebras, so f^*u ∪ f^*v = f^*(u ∪ v); and ξ has even degree, hence commutes with f^*u. Therefore
  β(f^*u, f^*v) = tr_S(f^*u ∪ ξ ∪ f^*v) = tr_S(ξ ∪ f^*u ∪ f^*v) = tr_S(ξ ∪ f^*(u ∪ v)).   (3.1)

Step 4: there is a nonzero constant c with tr_S(ξ ∪ f^*z) = c · tr_C(z) for all z ∈ H^2(C). Let L_H := O_S(H) be the line bundle of the F_q-rational very ample divisor H; it is an ample line bundle on S defined over F_q. Since H is a divisor on the smooth variety S, its cycle class ξ is the first Chern class of O_S(H): the cycle class map on codimension-one cycles is, by definition of the cycle class map (via the identification CH^1 ≅ Pic and the ℓ-adic first Chern class), the composite Pic(S) → H^2_ét(S, Q_ℓ(1)) given by c_1, so under the identification Q_ℓ(1) ≅ Q_ℓ the class c_1(L_H) ∈ H^2(S, Q_ℓ(1)) corresponds to ξ ∈ H^2(S).
Now apply lemma_247 to the morphism f : S → C. This is legitimate: S and C are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimensions D = 2 and E = 1 over F_q, so D ≥ E; f is a morphism of projective F_q-varieties, hence proper, and it is surjective by hypothesis; and L_H is an ample line bundle on S defined over F_q with first Chern class c_1(L_H) ∈ H^2(S, Q_ℓ(1)). Lemma_247 (with r = D - E = 1) yields a positive integer d such that
  deg_S(c_1(L_H) ∪ f^*u) = d · deg_C(u)   for every u ∈ H^2(C, Q_ℓ(1)),   (4.1)
where deg_S : H^4(S, Q_ℓ(2)) → Q_ℓ and deg_C : H^2(C, Q_ℓ(1)) → Q_ℓ are the degree maps sending the class of a closed point w to [κ(w) : F_q].
We now transport (4.1) through the identifications Q_ℓ(1) ≅ Q_ℓ and Q_ℓ(2) ≅ Q_ℓ. Under these identifications H^2(C, Q_ℓ(1)) is identified with H^2(C), H^4(S, Q_ℓ(2)) with H^4(S), the class c_1(L_H) with ξ, and f^*u with f^*z, where z ∈ H^2(C) is the image of u. Moreover deg_S agrees with tr_S: both are Q_ℓ-linear maps H^4(S) → Q_ℓ sending the class cl(w) of every closed point w to [κ(w) : F_q], and H^4(S) is one-dimensional over Q_ℓ with cl(w) ≠ 0 (because tr_S(cl(w)) = [κ(w) : F_q] ≠ 0), so two such linear maps coincide. Likewise deg_C agrees with tr_C on H^2(C): both are Q_ℓ-linear, both send cl(w) to [κ(w) : F_q], and H^2(C) is one-dimensional with cl(w) ≠ 0. Therefore (4.1) is equivalent to
  tr_S(ξ ∪ f^*z) = d · tr_C(z)   for every z ∈ H^2(C).   (4.2)
Thus the constant c := d satisfies the requirement, and c is a positive integer, so c ≠ 0 in Q_ℓ (the map Q ↪ Q_ℓ is injective).

Step 5: conclusion. Combining (3.1) and (4.2), for all u, v ∈ H^1(C) we have
  β(f^*u, f^*v) = tr_S(ξ ∪ f^*(u ∪ v)) = c · tr_C(u ∪ v) = c · ⟨u, v⟩_C.   (5.1)
Since c ≠ 0 and ⟨ , ⟩_C is perfect, the form (u, v) ↦ c⟨u, v⟩_C is a perfect pairing on H^1(C). Let Θ : H^1(C) → H^1(C)^*, Θ(v) := ⟨ · , v⟩_C, which is an isomorphism, and let (f^*)^* : H^1(C)^* → H^1(S)^* be the transpose of the isomorphism f^*, which is again an isomorphism. By (5.1), for every v ∈ H^1(C) and every u ∈ H^1(C),
  φ(f^*v)(f^*u) = β(f^*u, f^*v) = c · ⟨u, v⟩_C = c · ((f^*)^*Θ(v))(f^*u),
hence, since f^* is surjective, φ(f^*v) = c · (f^*)^*Θ(v). As f^* is also injective, this says φ = c · (f^*)^* ∘ Θ ∘ (f^*)^{-1}, a composite of isomorphisms; hence φ is an isomorphism, i.e. β is a perfect pairing on H^1(S). By (2.2), L : H^1(S) → H^3(S), L(y) = y ∪ ξ, is an isomorphism.

This is exactly the assertion of the lemma: the map H^1_ét(S_k, Q_ℓ) → H^3_ét(S_k, Q_ℓ), x ↦ x ∪ ξ, is an isomorphism. ∎

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, and put k = algebraic closure of 𝔽_q. Let X and Y be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over 𝔽_q. Let F_X, F_Y, and F_{X×Y} be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms (id×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^q, acting on étale cohomology with ℚ_ℓ-coefficients of X_k, Y_k, and (X×_{𝔽_q}Y)_k, respectively. Suppose that F_X is semisimple on H^n_ét(X_k,ℚ_ℓ) for every integer n≥0 and that F_Y is semisimple on H^n_ét(Y_k,ℚ_ℓ) for every integer n≥0. Then F_{X×Y} is semisimple on H^n_ét((X×_{𝔽_q}Y)_k,ℚ_ℓ) for every integer n≥0.
proof:
Notation. Throughout, for an $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Z$ put $Z_k=Z\times_{\mathbb F_q}k$ with $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, write $H^n(Z):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and let $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, and $F_Z:=(\operatorname{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ acting on $H^n(Z)$. By hypothesis $F_X$ is semisimple on $H^n(X)$ for all $n\ge0$ and $F_Y$ is semisimple on $H^n(Y)$ for all $n\ge0$. We must show that $F_{X\times Y}$ is semisimple on $H^n(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)$ for all $n\ge0$. Fix $n\ge0$; all arguments below are for this fixed $n$.

Step 1 (finiteness and invertibility of the operators). The varieties $X$, $Y$ and $X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y$ are smooth projective, hence proper, over $\mathbb F_q$. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob) to each of them with $K$ the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $Z_k$, which lies in $D^b_c(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism; the lemma gives that $H^m(Z)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space for every $m\ge0$ and every $Z\in\{X,Y,X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y\}$. Next, by lemma_6a (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a), for every $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Z$ the pullback $F_Z=(\operatorname{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^m(Z)$ with inverse $(\operatorname{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*$, and in particular it is invertible whenever $H^m(Z)$ is finite-dimensional. Consequently, for all $m\ge0$,
$$F_X\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\big(H^m(X)\big),\qquad F_Y\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\big(H^m(Y)\big),\qquad F_{X\times Y}\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\big(H^m(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)\big).$$

Step 2 (Künneth decomposition compatible with Frobenius). Since $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective over $\mathbb F_q$, lemma_146 (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_146) applies and states: for every $m\ge0$ the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map
$$\Phi_m:\bigoplus_{i+j=m}H^i(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^j(Y)\longrightarrow H^m(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y),\qquad x\otimes y\mapsto \operatorname{pr}_1^*(x)\cup\operatorname{pr}_2^*(y),$$
is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and under $\Phi_m$ the operator $F_{X\times Y}$ corresponds to $F_X\otimes F_Y$ on the $(i,j)$-summand, for all $i,j\ge0$; that is, if $\iota_{i,j}$ denotes the inclusion of the $(i,j)$-summand into the direct sum, then
$$\Phi_m\circ\iota_{i,j}\circ\big(F_X|_{H^i(X)}\otimes F_Y|_{H^j(Y)}\big)=F_{X\times Y}\circ\Phi_m\circ\iota_{i,j}\qquad\text{for all }i,j\ge0. \tag{1}$$
Equivalently, $\Phi_m\circ T_m=F_{X\times Y}\circ\Phi_m$ where $T_m:=\bigoplus_{i+j=m}\big(F_X|_{H^i(X)}\otimes F_Y|_{H^j(Y)}\big)$ is the direct-sum operator on $\bigoplus_{i+j=m}H^i(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^j(Y)$.

Step 3 (each summand is semisimple). Fix $i,j\ge0$. By Step 1, $H^i(X)$ and $H^j(Y)$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces and $F_X|_{H^i(X)}$, $F_Y|_{H^j(Y)}$ are invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operators. By hypothesis $F_X$ is semisimple on $H^i(X)$ and $F_Y$ is semisimple on $H^j(Y)$. Hence lemma_147 (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_147) applies and yields that
$$F_X|_{H^i(X)}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}F_Y|_{H^j(Y)}$$
is a semisimple $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of the finite-dimensional space $H^i(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^j(Y)$.

Step 4 (the finite direct sum is semisimple). For the fixed $n$, the index set $\{(i,j)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2 : i+j=n\}$ is finite, of cardinality $n+1$; enumerate it as $(i_1,j_1),\dots,(i_{n+1},j_{n+1})$. By Step 1 each $V_r:=H^{i_r}(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{j_r}(Y)$ is finite-dimensional and each $S_r:=F_X|_{H^{i_r}(X)}\otimes F_Y|_{H^{j_r}(Y)}$ is an invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator on $V_r$ (a tensor product of invertible operators is invertible, with inverse the tensor product of the inverses), and by Step 3 each $S_r$ is semisimple. Lemma_9 (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9) applied to the finite family $(V_r,S_r)_{r=1}^{n+1}$ therefore gives that
$$T_n=\bigoplus_{r=1}^{n+1}S_r=\bigoplus_{i+j=n}\big(F_X|_{H^i(X)}\otimes F_Y|_{H^j(Y)}\big)$$
is semisimple on $\bigoplus_{i+j=n}H^i(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^j(Y)$.

Step 5 (transport of semisimplicity across the Künneth isomorphism). By Step 2, $\Phi_n$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism intertwining $T_n$ with $F_{X\times Y}|_{H^n(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)}$, i.e. $\Phi_n\circ T_n=F_{X\times Y}\circ\Phi_n$. Both $T_n$ (a direct sum of invertible operators, hence invertible) and $F_{X\times Y}|_{H^n(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)}$ (Step 1) are invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operators on finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces. Lemma_8 (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8), applied with $\alpha=\Phi_n$, $T_V=T_n$ and $T_W=F_{X\times Y}|_{H^n(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)}$, now gives: $T_n$ is semisimple if and only if $F_{X\times Y}|_{H^n(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)}$ is semisimple. Since $T_n$ is semisimple by Step 4, $F_{X\times Y}$ is semisimple on $H^n(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)$.

Conclusion. The integer $n\ge0$ was arbitrary, so $F_{X\times Y}$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n\ge0$, as required. (We note that the hypothesis of geometric connectedness was not needed anywhere; smoothness and projectivity of $X$ and $Y$ were used only to have properness, for finite-dimensionality via lemma_45_finite_frob, and to apply the Künneth theorem lemma_146.)

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, and put k = algebraic closure of 𝔽_q. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d≥1 over 𝔽_q, let Y⊂X be a smooth ample divisor defined over 𝔽_q, and put U=X∖Y. Let F be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism (id×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^q, acting on H^n_ét(X_k,ℚ_ℓ), on H^n_ét(Y_k,ℚ_ℓ), and on H^n_{c,ét}(U_k,ℚ_ℓ) for every n≥0. Suppose that F is semisimple on H^n_ét(Y_k,ℚ_ℓ) for every n≥0, that F is semisimple on H^n_{c,ét}(U_k,ℚ_ℓ) for every n≥0, and that for every n≥0 the characteristic polynomial of F on H^n_ét(Y_k,ℚ_ℓ) is coprime in ℚ_ℓ[t] to the characteristic polynomial of F on H^n_{c,ét}(U_k,ℚ_ℓ). Then F is semisimple on H^n_ét(X_k,ℚ_ℓ) for every n≥0.
proof:
Notation. Fix n ≥ 0 and put
 A^n := H^n_{c,ét}(U_k, Q_ℓ),  B^n := H^n_{ét}(X_k, Q_ℓ),  C^n := H^n_{ét}(Y_k, Q_ℓ).
All three are finite dimensional over Q_ℓ (this is part of the conclusion of the long exact sequence quoted below). The q-power arithmetic Frobenius F = (id × Spec σ)^*, σ(c) = c^q, is induced by the automorphism id_{X_k} × Spec σ of X_k = X ×_{F_q} k over k (and likewise for Y_k and U_k), hence acts as an automorphism of each of these Q_ℓ-vector spaces; in particular F ∈ GL_{Q_ℓ}(A^n), GL_{Q_ℓ}(B^n), GL_{Q_ℓ}(C^n).

Step 1 (the Frobenius-equivariant localisation sequence). The variety X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d ≥ 1 over F_q, and Y ⊂ X is a smooth ample divisor defined over F_q. Since X is smooth, it is locally factorial, so the closed subvariety Y, being of pure codimension one in the pure-dimensional X, is an effective Cartier divisor on X; it is smooth, hence of pure dimension d−1, and it is ample by hypothesis. Thus the hypotheses of Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_283 are satisfied, and we obtain a long exact sequence of finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector spaces
 ··· → A^n → B^n → C^n → A^{n+1} → B^{n+1} → ···
in which the map B^n → C^n is the pullback i^*_n along the closed immersion i: Y ↪ X, and in which every map commutes with the q-power arithmetic Frobenius on the four terms. Write α_n : A^n → B^n and β_n := i^*_n : B^n → C^n for the two maps starting at B^n.

Step 2 (exactness at B^n, and stability). By exactness of the sequence at B^n,
 ker(β_n) = im(α_n).
Since α_n and β_n commute with F, the subspace im(α_n) ⊆ B^n is F-stable, and so is ker(β_n) = im(α_n); likewise im(β_n) ⊆ C^n is F-stable (F(im β_n) = im(F ∘ β_n) = im(β_n ∘ F) = im(β_n), using that F is bijective). We therefore have two F-equivariant exact sequences of finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector spaces
 (a) 0 → ker(α_n) → A^n → im(α_n) → 0,  so im(α_n) ≅ A^n/ker(α_n) as F-modules;
 (b) 0 → im(α_n) = ker(β_n) → B^n → im(β_n) → 0,
where in (b) the subspace im(α_n) is F-stable and the quotient im(β_n) carries the operator induced by F, which coincides with the restriction F|_{im(β_n)} because im(β_n) is F-stable in C^n.

Step 3 (semisimplicity of F on the two outer pieces).
(i) By hypothesis F is semisimple on A^n. The subspace ker(α_n) is F-stable, so by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_402 the operator induced by F on the quotient A^n/ker(α_n) is semisimple; via the F-equivariant isomorphism of Step 2(a) this says that F is semisimple on im(α_n).
(ii) By hypothesis F is semisimple on C^n. The subspace im(β_n) is F-stable, so by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515 the restriction F|_{im(β_n)} is semisimple.

Step 4 (a characteristic-polynomial fact, proved here). Claim: if V is a finite-dimensional vector space over a field K, T ∈ GL_K(V), and W ⊆ V is a T-stable subspace with induced operator T̄ on V/W, then χ_T = χ_{T|_W} · χ_{T̄} in K[t]; in particular χ_{T|_W} divides χ_T and χ_{T̄} divides χ_T.
Proof of the claim: choose a K-basis (w_1,…,w_r) of W and extend it to a basis (w_1,…,w_r,v_{r+1},…,v_m) of V. Since W is T-stable, the matrix of T in this basis is block upper triangular, [T] = ( A  C ; 0  D ), where A is the matrix of T|_W in the basis (w_i) and D is the matrix of T̄ in the basis given by the images of the v_j. Hence χ_T(t) = det(t·I_m − [T]) = det(t·I_r − A) · det(t·I_{m−r} − D) = χ_{T|_W}(t) · χ_{T̄}(t), using the multiplicativity of the determinant on block upper triangular matrices. (For the zero space the characteristic polynomial is 1 by the usual convention, and the identity remains valid.)

Step 5 (coprimality of the two outer characteristic polynomials). By Step 4 applied to (a), χ_{F on im(α_n)} divides χ_{F on A^n} in Q_ℓ[t]. By Step 4 applied to the F-stable subspace im(β_n) of C^n, χ_{F on im(β_n)} divides χ_{F on C^n} in Q_ℓ[t]. By hypothesis, for our fixed n the characteristic polynomial of F on C^n = H^n_{ét}(Y_k, Q_ℓ) is coprime in Q_ℓ[t] to the characteristic polynomial of F on A^n = H^n_{c,ét}(U_k, Q_ℓ). Since a divisor of a polynomial coprime to a divisor of a coprime polynomial is again coprime, χ_{F on im(α_n)} and χ_{F on im(β_n)} are coprime in Q_ℓ[t].

Step 6 (assembling). We apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_227 to the F-equivariant exact sequence of Step 2(b),
 0 → V' := im(α_n) → V := B^n → V'' := im(β_n) → 0,
with T := F ∈ GL_{Q_ℓ}(B^n). Its hypotheses are verified: V' is F-stable, V'' = B^n/V' carries the induced automorphism (which is F|_{im(β_n)}), F|_{V'} is semisimple by Step 3(i), F|_{V''} is semisimple by Step 3(ii), and their characteristic polynomials are coprime by Step 5. The conclusion is that F is semisimple on V = B^n = H^n_{ét}(X_k, Q_ℓ).

Degenerate cases. If A^n = 0 then im(α_n) = 0, its characteristic polynomial is 1, and the same argument (or directly Step 3(ii) together with B^n ≅ im(β_n)) gives semisimplicity of F on B^n; similarly if C^n = 0 then im(β_n) = 0 and B^n = im(α_n) is a quotient of A^n, semisimple by Step 3(i). Both are instances of the argument above, since the zero space is semisimple and its characteristic polynomial 1 is coprime to every polynomial.

Since n ≥ 0 was arbitrary, F is semisimple on H^n_{ét}(X_k, Q_ℓ) for every n ≥ 0, as required.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, and put k = algebraic closure of 𝔽_q. Let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over 𝔽_q. Fix a nonzero element of ℚ_ℓ(1) and use it to identify Tate twists with ℚ_ℓ. Suppose that there exists an integer r≥1 such that H^2_ét(S_k,ℚ_ℓ) is spanned over ℚ_ℓ by the cycle classes of the divisors on S defined over 𝔽_{q^r}. Then the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism (id×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^q, is semisimple on H^n_ét(S_k,ℚ_ℓ) for every integer n≥0.
proof:
Let F=(id×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^q, be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius. We prove semisimplicity of F on each H^n_et(S_k,Q_l).

Step 1: n=2. Let A_r be the Q_l-subspace of H^2_et(S_k,Q_l) spanned by the cycle classes of Cartier divisors on S_{F_{q^r}}. Since S is a smooth surface, every divisor on S_{F_{q^r}} is Cartier, so the hypothesis says exactly that H^2_et(S_k,Q_l)=A_r. By lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/d9031b, F is semisimple on A_r. Hence F is semisimple on H^2_et(S_k,Q_l).

Step 2: n=1. By lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/ec0b56, the q-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^1_et(S_k,Q_l).

Step 3: n=3. Since S has pure dimension 2, lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_107 with d=2 gives an F-equivariant identification of H^3_et(S_k,Q_l) with the dual, twisted, of H^1_et(S_k,Q_l), and in particular states that F is semisimple on H^1 if and only if it is semisimple on H^3. Since Step 2 gives semisimplicity on H^1, F is semisimple on H^3_et(S_k,Q_l).

Step 4: n=4. By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_199 with D=2, F acts on H^4_et(S_k,Q_l) as multiplication by q^2. Since q is invertible in Q_l, q^2 is a nonzero scalar, so F is semisimple there.

Step 5: n=0. Since S is geometrically connected, S_k is connected. Therefore H^0_et(S_k,Q_l)=Γ(S_k,Q_l)=Q_l. The pullback F^* sends the constant global section 1 to 1, so F acts as the identity on H^0_et(S_k,Q_l). The identity operator is semisimple.

Step 6: n>4. The variety S_k is projective and equidimensional of dimension 2. By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_projective_cohomology_vanishes_above_twice_dimension, H^n_et(S_k,Q_l)=0 for every n>4. The zero vector space carries the zero operator, which is semisimple.

Thus for every integer n≥0, F is semisimple on H^n_et(S_k,Q_l), as required.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_q\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\beta(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)\) be the Poincaré duality trace pairing on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), where \(\operatorname{tr}_S\) is normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_S(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\) for closed points \(z\) of \(S\). Let \(A\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear span in \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) of the cycle classes of the divisors on \(S_k\), and put \(T=A^{\perp}\) with respect to \(\beta\). Suppose that \(\beta|_A\) is nondegenerate and that \(\beta|_T\) is positive definite or negative definite. Then the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), is semisimple on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
Let V = H^2_et(S_k,Q_l), and let F = (id_{S_k} × Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^q, be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius. By lemma_6a, F is a Q_l-linear automorphism of V; by lemma_45_finite_frob, V is finite-dimensional.

The trace tr_S is the Poincaré duality trace of lemma_77(a) for m=1 and d=2: it is the map H^4_et(S_k,Q_l) → Q_l(-2) ≅ Q_l, normalized by tr_S(cl(z)) = [κ(z):F_q]. By lemma_77(b) with n=2, d=2, m=1, the pairing β(x,y)=tr_S(x∪y) is perfect, and β(Fx,Fy)=q^2 β(x,y) for all x,y∈V. It is symmetric because x∪y = (-1)^{2·2} y∪x = y∪x in H^4.

Let A be the Q_l-span of the cycle classes of divisors on S_k, and T=A^⊥. By 9db8b3 (with m=1), F(A)⊆A and F(T)⊆T.

We first record that A equals one of the spaces A_r appearing in d9031b. For r≥1 let A_r be the Q_l-span of the cycle classes of Cartier divisors on S_{F_{q^r}}. Claim: A = A_R for some R≥1. Indeed, let D be any divisor on S_k. Write D = Σ n_j Z_j with Z_j prime divisors. Since S is of finite type over F_q, choose a finite affine cover of S by spectra of finitely generated F_q-algebras. On the induced affine cover of S_k, the ideal sheaf of each Z_j is generated by finitely many functions; the finitely many coefficients of these functions in k lie in some finite subfield F_{q^{r_j}} of k. Hence Z_j, and therefore D, is defined over some finite extension F_{q^R}. (Equivalently, the coherent ideal sheaf of D is defined by finitely many equations with coefficients in k.) Thus cl(D) lies in A_R for some R. Since A is finite-dimensional (it is a subspace of V), choose a basis a_1,...,a_m of A. Each a_i is a finite Q_l-linear combination of cycle classes of divisors, each defined over some finite extension; taking R to be a common multiple of the finitely many extensions involved, we get a_i∈A_R for all i. Hence A⊆A_R. Conversely, every divisor on S_{F_{q^R}} base-changes to a divisor on S_k, so A_R⊆A. Therefore A=A_R. Since S is smooth, every divisor on S_{F_{q^R}} is Cartier, so this is exactly the space A_R of d9031b. Applying d9031b with r=R, we conclude that F is semisimple on A.

Next we show that β|_T is nondegenerate and that V=A⊕T. Since β|_A is nondegenerate, A∩A^⊥=0. The map φ:V→A^*, φ(v)(a)=β(v,a), is surjective: β identifies V with V^*, and restriction V^*→A^* is surjective. Its kernel is T, so dim V = dim A + dim T; hence V=A⊕T. If t∈T and β(t,T)=0, then for v=a+t' with a∈A and t'∈T we have β(t,v)=β(t,a)+β(t,t')=0, so t∈V^⊥=0 because β is perfect. Thus β|_T is nondegenerate.

Now apply lemma_364 to the finite-dimensional Q_l-space T, the operator F|_T, the nondegenerate symmetric form B=β|_T, and c=q^2∈Q_l^×. The restriction F|_T is an automorphism of T: F(T)⊆T and F is injective on the finite-dimensional space T. For x,y∈T we have B(Fx,Fy)=β(Fx,Fy)=q^2β(x,y)=q^2B(x,y). The hypothesis that β|_T is positive definite or negative definite is precisely the hypothesis, for the symmetric Q_l-bilinear form B, that for some field embedding σ:Qbar_l→C the induced Hermitian form on T⊗_{Q_l,σ}C is positive definite or negative definite (if the hypothesis is stated for every embedding, choose any one). Hence lemma_364 gives that F|_T is semisimple. If T=0 this is vacuous and the same conclusion holds.

Finally apply lemma_479 with K=Q_l, V=H^2_et(S_k,Q_l), B=β, c=q^2, operator F, and W=A. All hypotheses are satisfied: K has characteristic 0, V is finite-dimensional, β is a perfect symmetric bilinear form, c=q^2 is nonzero, β(Fv,Fw)=q^2β(v,w) for all v,w∈V, A is F-stable, and β|_A is nondegenerate. Lemma_479 says that F is semisimple on V if and only if it is semisimple on A and on A^⊥=T. We have proved both. Therefore F is semisimple on H^2_et(S_k,Q_l), as required.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, and put k = algebraic closure of 𝔽_q. Let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over 𝔽_q that is isomorphic to a product C_1×_{𝔽_q}⋯×_{𝔽_q}C_M of smooth projective geometrically connected curves C_1,…,C_M over 𝔽_q with M≥2. Let Z⊂Y be a smooth closed subvariety of pure codimension 2 defined over 𝔽_q, and suppose that Z is isomorphic over 𝔽_q to a product of finitely many smooth projective geometrically connected curves over 𝔽_q (where the empty product is Spec 𝔽_q). Let π:X=Bl_Z Y→Y be the blow-up of Y along Z. Then the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism (id_{X_k}×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^q, is semisimple on H^n_ét(X_k,ℚ_ℓ) for every integer n≥0.
proof:
Proof. We first record a transfer fact. Let V and W be smooth projective varieties over F_q and let φ: V → W be an F_q-isomorphism. For each n put A_n = H^n_et(V_k, Q_l), B_n = H^n_et(W_k, Q_l), and let F_V, F_W be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms. The base change φ_k: V_k → W_k is an isomorphism, so α = φ_k^*: B_n → A_n is a Q_l-linear isomorphism. Since φ is defined over F_q, the diagram
V_k --φ_k--> W_k
| id_V × Spec σ          | id_W × Spec σ
v                        v
V_k --φ_k--> W_k
commutes; hence α ∘ F_W = F_V ∘ α. The spaces A_n and B_n are finite-dimensional by lemma_45_finite_frob, applied to the constant sheaf Q_l on the proper varieties V and W, and F_V and F_W are invertible by lemma_6a. Therefore lemma_8 gives that F_V is semisimple on A_n if and only if F_W is semisimple on B_n. We shall use this fact twice.

Step 1: Semisimplicity on Y. By hypothesis there is an F_q-isomorphism φ_Y: Y → Y' = C_1 × ... × C_M with M ≥ 2. Each C_i is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_q. Lemma_341, applied to C_1,...,C_M, says that the q-power arithmetic Frobenius F_{Y'} is semisimple on H^n_et(Y'_k, Q_l) for every n ≥ 0. Note that lemma_341 has no hypothesis that the product Y' be geometrically connected; we neither assert nor need that. Applying the transfer fact to φ_Y gives that F_Y is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k, Q_l) for every n ≥ 0.

Step 2: Semisimplicity on Z. By hypothesis there is an F_q-isomorphism ψ: Z → Z', where Z' is a product of N smooth projective geometrically connected curves over F_q, with N ≥ 0, and the empty product is Spec F_q. If N ≥ 1, write Z' = C'_1 × ... × C'_N. Lemma_341 applied to C'_1,...,C'_N gives semisimplicity of F_{Z'} on H^n_et(Z'_k, Q_l) for all n ≥ 0; the transfer fact applied to ψ gives semisimplicity of F_Z on H^n_et(Z_k, Q_l) for all n ≥ 0. Again no geometric connectedness of Z' is used. If N = 0, then Z ≅ Spec F_q over F_q, so Z_k ≅ Spec k. Since k is algebraically closed, it is a strictly henselian local ring, and the identity morphism Spec k → Spec k is finite. By lemma_finite_over_strictly_henselian_exact, the global sections functor on the small étale site of Spec k is exact. Hence H^0_et(Spec k, Q_l) = Q_l and H^n_et(Spec k, Q_l) = 0 for n > 0. The arithmetic Frobenius on Spec k fixes the global section 1, so it acts trivially on H^0 and is semisimple; on the zero spaces it is semisimple vacuously. Thus F_Z is semisimple on H^n_et(Z_k, Q_l) for every n ≥ 0 in all cases.

Step 3: Blow-up. The variety Y is smooth projective geometrically connected over F_q and is isomorphic to a product of M ≥ 2 curves, so it has pure dimension M ≥ 2. The center Z is a smooth closed subvariety of pure codimension 2 defined over F_q. Let X = Bl_Z Y, with blow-up map π: X → Y. Apply lemma_4ca7f1 with m = 1, ambient variety Y, center Z, and blow-up X. It gives, for every integer n ≥ 0, that the q-power arithmetic Frobenius F is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_l) if and only if it is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k, Q_l) and on H^{n-2}_et(Z_k, Q_l), where H^j_et(Z_k, Q_l) = 0 for j < 0. The first condition holds for every n by Step 1. The second holds for every n by Step 2, with the convention that H^j = 0 for j < 0 and that the zero operator on the zero space is semisimple. Therefore F is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_l) for every n ≥ 0. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_q\) and let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_q\). Let \(F_S\) be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and let \(F_A\) be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Suppose there exists a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear injection \(\iota:H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) such that \(\iota\circ F_S=(F_A\otimes F_A)\circ\iota\) and such that \(\iota\bigl(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\) is a direct summand of the tensor product as a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space. Then \(F_S\) is semisimple on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
Throughout, $q=p^a$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\neq p$, and all tensor products are over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ unless indicated otherwise. Write
\[
V:=H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad H:=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad W:=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H,
\]
and let
\[
T:=F_S\in \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V),\qquad U:=F_A\otimes F_A\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W)
\]
be the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operators in question. The hypothesis gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear injection $\iota\colon V\hookrightarrow W$ with
\[
\iota\circ T=U\circ \iota .\tag{1}
\]
We prove that $T$ is semisimple on $V$ in five steps.

**Step 1 (finite-dimensionality).** $S$ is smooth projective, hence proper, over $\mathbb F_q$; likewise an abelian variety $A$ over $\mathbb F_q$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$. Take the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $S_k$ (resp.\ on $A_k$), which is an object of $D^b_c$ carrying its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell$. Applying the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob with $X=S$ and with $X=A$ shows that $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ are finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ for every $n\ge 0$. In particular $V=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V<\infty$ and $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H<\infty$, hence $W=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H$ is finite-dimensional, with $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W=(\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H)^2$.

**Step 2 (invertibility).** Since $V$ and $H$ are finite-dimensional, the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a shows that the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius pullbacks $F_S=(\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ and $F_A=(\operatorname{id}_{A_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms of $V$ and of $H$ respectively. Consequently $U=F_A\otimes F_A$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $W$, with inverse $F_A^{-1}\otimes F_A^{-1}$; explicitly, for $x,y\in H$, $(F_A^{-1}\otimes F_A^{-1})\bigl(U(x\otimes y)\bigr)=(F_A^{-1}\otimes F_A^{-1})(F_Ax\otimes F_Ay)=x\otimes y$. Thus $T\in \mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$ and $U\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W)$.

**Step 3 ($U$ is semisimple on $W$).** By the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_h1_abelian_semisimple, the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $F_A$ is semisimple on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H$. The field $\mathbb Q_\ell$ has characteristic $0$, so the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_590 (applied with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$, with $V=W=H$ and with $T=S=F_A$) shows that
\[
U=F_A\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}F_A\ \text{is semisimple on}\ W=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H.
\]
(Here we use that $F_A$ is an automorphism, which is Step 2, so that $F_A\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H)$ as required by that lemma.)

**Step 4 ($U$ restricted to $\iota(V)$ is semisimple).** We claim that the subspace $\iota(V)\subseteq W$ is $U$-stable. Indeed, let $v\in V$. By (1), $\iota(Tv)=U(\iota v)$, and $Tv\in V$, so $U(\iota v)=\iota(Tv)\in\iota(V)$. Hence $U(\iota(V))\subseteq \iota(V)$. Applying the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515 with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$, with $W$ there equal to our $W$, with $T$ there equal to $U$, and with the $T$-stable subspace equal to $\iota(V)$, we conclude:
\[
U|_{\iota(V)}\ \text{is semisimple on}\ \iota(V).
\]

**Step 5 (transport back to $V$).** The map $\iota$ is injective by hypothesis, so it induces a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\iota\colon V\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\iota(V)$. Moreover $U|_{\iota(V)}$ is an automorphism of $\iota(V)$: since $T$ is surjective (Step 2), $U(\iota(V))=\iota(T(V))=\iota(V)$, so $U|_{\iota(V)}$ is a surjective endomorphism of the finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\iota(V)$, hence bijective. Equation (1) says precisely that
\[
\iota\circ T=(U|_{\iota(V)})\circ\iota
\]
as $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps $V\to\iota(V)$. We now apply the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8 with $T_V:=T\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$, $T_W:=U|_{\iota(V)}\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(\iota(V))$ and $\alpha:=\iota$: it yields that $T$ is semisimple on $V$ if and only if $U|_{\iota(V)}$ is semisimple on $\iota(V)$. The latter holds by Step 4, hence
\[
F_S=T\ \text{is semisimple on}\ H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=V,
\]
which is the assertion of the lemma.

**Remark.** The hypothesis that $\iota\bigl(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)$ be a direct summand of $H^1\otimes H^1$ as a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space is not needed for the argument above: semisimplicity of $U$ on the whole tensor product together with $U$-stability of the image is enough (Step 4). With the direct-summand hypothesis one could alternatively invoke the restriction statement for $T$-stable direct summands, but the conclusion is the same.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, let \(r\ge1\) be an integer, let \(V\) be a two-dimensional \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-vector space with basis \(e_1,e_2\), let \(\beta\) be the alternating bilinear form on \(V\) determined by \(\beta(e_1,e_2)=1\), let \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) satisfy \(\alpha^2=q^r\), and let \(F\in\mathrm{GL}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}(V)\) be given by \(F(e_1)=\alpha e_1\) and \(F(e_2)=\alpha(e_1+e_2)\). Then \(\beta(Fx,Fy)=q^r\beta(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in V\), and \(F\) is not semisimple on \(V\).
proof:
Let \(x=a e_1+b e_2\) and \(y=c e_1+d e_2\). Since \(\beta\) is alternating with \(\beta(e_1,e_2)=1\), we have
\[
\beta(x,y)=ad-bc.
\]
Also
\[
F(x)=a\alpha e_1+b\alpha(e_1+e_2)=\alpha(a+b)e_1+\alpha b e_2,
\]
and similarly
\[
F(y)=\alpha(c+d)e_1+\alpha d e_2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\beta(Fx,Fy)=\alpha^2\bigl((a+b)d-b(c+d)\bigr)
=\alpha^2(ad-bc)
=q^r\beta(x,y),
\]
using \(\alpha^2=q^r\). This proves the first assertion.

For the second assertion, note that \(\alpha\neq0\) because \(\alpha^2=q^r\) and \(q=p^a\neq0\) in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) (as \(\ell\neq p\)). The matrix of \(F\) in the basis \((e_1,e_2)\) is
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha & \alpha\\ 0 & \alpha\end{pmatrix},
\]
so its characteristic polynomial is \((T-\alpha)^2\). Thus \(\alpha\) is the only eigenvalue of \(F\). Put \(N=F-\alpha\operatorname{id}_V\). Then \(N(e_1)=0\) and \(N(e_2)=\alpha e_1\), so \(N\neq0\), while \(N^2=0\).

If \(F\) were semisimple, then over the algebraically closed field \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) it would be diagonalizable. Since its only eigenvalue is \(\alpha\), any diagonal matrix similar to \(F\) would be \(\alpha I\), hence \(F=\alpha\operatorname{id}_V\). But
\[
F(e_2)=\alpha(e_1+e_2)\neq \alpha e_2
\]
because \(\alpha e_1\neq0\), a contradiction. Equivalently, the minimal polynomial of \(F\) is \((T-\alpha)^2\), which has a repeated root and is not squarefree. Therefore \(F\) is not semisimple on \(V\).

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, let m≥1 be an integer, and put k=F̄_q. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d≥2 over F_{q^m}, and let Y⊂X be a smooth ample divisor defined over F_{q^m}. Suppose that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_ét(Y_k,Q_ℓ) for every integer n≥0. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_ét(X_k,Q_ℓ) for every integer n with 0≤n≤d−1.
proof: Let F_X and F_Y denote the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms on H^n_ét(X_k,Q_ℓ) and H^n_ét(Y_k,Q_ℓ), respectively, and let i:Y→X be the closed immersion. Since X is smooth, Y is a Cartier divisor. Since Y is ample and X is a positive-dimensional projective variety, Y is nonempty (if Y were empty, then O_X(Y)≅O_X, which is not ample). Thus lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc applies. It gives, for every integer n, that i^*:H^n_ét(X_k,Q_ℓ)→H^n_ét(Y_k,Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism for n≤d−2 and is injective for n=d−1, and that i^*∘F_X=F_Y∘i^*. Fix n with 0≤n≤d−1. If n≤d−2, then i^* is an isomorphism intertwining F_X and F_Y, so F_X=(i^*)^{-1}∘F_Y∘i^*. Conjugation by a linear isomorphism preserves the minimal polynomial, hence preserves semisimplicity; since F_Y is semisimple by hypothesis, F_X is semisimple. If n=d−1, put W=i^*(H^{d−1}_ét(X_k,Q_ℓ))⊂H^{d−1}_ét(Y_k,Q_ℓ). The equivariance i^*∘F_X=F_Y∘i^* shows that W is F_Y-stable. By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515 applied to V=H^{d−1}_ét(Y_k,Q_ℓ), T=F_Y, and the stable subspace W, the restriction F_Y|_W is semisimple. The map i^*:H^{d−1}_ét(X_k,Q_ℓ)→W is an isomorphism of Q_ℓ-vector spaces and satisfies i^*∘F_X=(F_Y|_W)∘i^*, so F_X=(i^*)^{-1}∘(F_Y|_W)∘i^* is conjugate to F_Y|_W and is therefore semisimple. The two cases n≤d−2 and n=d−1 cover all integers n with 0≤n≤d−1. Hence F_X is semisimple on H^n_ét(X_k,Q_ℓ) for every such n.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(Y\subset S\) be a smooth ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), and put \(U=S\setminus Y\). Then \(H^1_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\).
proof: Let k be an algebraic closure of F_q. Fix a nonzero element of Q_l(1) and use it to identify all Tate twists with Q_l; this is only a bookkeeping device and does not affect the vanishing statement. All cohomology below has Q_l coefficients. Write i:Y_k -> S_k and j:U_k -> S_k for the inclusions. Step 1: U_k is smooth affine of pure dimension 2, H^m_et(U_k)=0 for every m>2, and H^0_{c,et}(U_k)=0. Since Y is a nonempty proper ample divisor on S, its base change Y_k is a nonempty proper closed subscheme of S_k defined by a section of the ample line bundle O_{S_k}(Y_k). Applying lemma_337 with X=S_k, L=O_{S_k}(Y_k), d=2, gives that U_k is affine of Krull dimension 2 and H^m_et(U_k)=0 for every integer m>2. In particular H^3_et(U_k)=0. The open subscheme U_k of the smooth surface S_k is smooth of pure dimension 2, so lemma_hc_zero_smooth_affine_positive_dimension gives H^0_{c,et}(U_k)=0. Step 2: Y_k is connected. Suppose Y_k has at least two connected components. Since Y_k is smooth over the algebraically closed field k, its connected components Y_1,...,Y_r with r>=2 are pairwise disjoint smooth projective integral curves, and Y_k=sum_i Y_i as a reduced divisor. The divisor Y_k is ample on S_k (ampleness is stable under base field extension). Hence for each i we have Y_i·Y_k>0: indeed some positive multiple mY_k is very ample, and then m(Y_i·Y_k)=deg(O(mY_k)|_{Y_i})>0 because O(mY_k)|_{Y_i} is ample on the curve Y_i. Since the components are disjoint, Y_i·Y_k=Y_i^2, so Y_i^2>0. Put a=Y_2^2>0 and b=Y_1^2>0, and let D=aY_1-bY_2. Then D·Y_k=aY_1·Y_k-bY_2·Y_k=aY_1^2-bY_2^2=ab-ba=0. Since Y_k is ample, lemma_surface_hodge_index with H=Y_k gives D^2<=0. But D^2 = a^2 Y_1^2 - 2ab (Y_1·Y_2) + b^2 Y_2^2 = a^2 b + b^2 a = ab(a+b) > 0, since Y_1·Y_2=0 and a,b>0. This contradicts D^2<=0, so Y_k is connected. Step 3: the restriction map H^0_et(S_k,Q_l) -> H^0_et(Y_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism. Indeed S_k is connected, so H^0_et(S_k,Q_l)=Q_l; Y_k is connected, so H^0_et(Y_k,Q_l)=Q_l; and i^* sends the class 1 to the class 1. Step 4: i^*:H^1_et(S_k,Q_l) -> H^1_et(Y_k,Q_l) is injective. Let z in H^1_et(S_k,Q_l) with i^*z=0. By lemma_77 (with d=2 and n=1) the pairing H^1_et(S_k,Q_l) x H^3_et(S_k,Q_l) -> Q_l, (x,y) |-> tr_S(x cup y), is perfect, where tr_S is the Poincare duality trace. Hence it suffices to prove tr_S(z cup w)=0 for every w in H^3_et(S_k,Q_l). By the Gysin sequence of lemma_ordinary_gysin_sequence_open_complement in degree 3, namely H^1_et(Y_k,Q_l)(-1) --i_!-> H^3_et(S_k,Q_l) --j^*-> H^3_et(U_k,Q_l), and by H^3_et(U_k,Q_l)=0 from Step 1, the Gysin map i_! is surjective. Thus w=i_! a for some a in H^1_et(Y_k,Q_l)(-1). Using the identification of Tate twists with Q_l and the Gysin projection formula (lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor), there is a nonzero constant c in Q_l^× such that tr_S(i_! a cup z)=c tr_Y(a cup i^* z) for all a and z; the sign possibly produced by graded commutativity is absorbed into c. Since i^*z=0, the right side is 0, hence tr_S(w cup z)=0 (up to the nonzero sign from commuting w and z). Therefore tr_S(z cup w)=0 for all w, and perfectness gives z=0. So i^* is injective on H^1. Step 5: apply the compact-support localization sequence of lemma_283 to the pair (S,Y). In low degrees it reads H^0_{c,et}(U_k,Q_l) -> H^0_et(S_k,Q_l) -> H^0_et(Y_k,Q_l) -> H^1_{c,et}(U_k,Q_l) -> H^1_et(S_k,Q_l) -> H^1_et(Y_k,Q_l). By Step 1, H^0_{c,et}(U_k,Q_l)=0. By Step 3, the map H^0_et(S_k,Q_l) -> H^0_et(Y_k,Q_l) is surjective. Exactness at H^0_et(Y_k,Q_l) then shows that the map H^0_et(Y_k,Q_l) -> H^1_{c,et}(U_k,Q_l) is zero, so H^1_{c,et}(U_k,Q_l) -> H^1_et(S_k,Q_l) is injective. Exactness at H^1_{c,et}(U_k,Q_l) identifies the image of this map with the kernel of H^1_et(S_k,Q_l) -> H^1_et(Y_k,Q_l), which is zero by Step 4. Hence H^1_{c,et}(U_k,Q_l)=0, as required.

statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}V^n\) be a finite-dimensional graded associative \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-algebra with unit \(1\in V^0\), and let \(F\) be an automorphism of \(V\) as a graded \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-algebra. Suppose that there exist homogeneous elements \(s_1,\dots,s_r\in V\) such that \(V\) is generated as a graded \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-algebra by \(1,s_1,\dots,s_r\), and such that for every \(i\) the restriction of \(F\) to the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear span of \(\{F^m s_i : m\ge0\}\) is semisimple. Then \(F\) is semisimple on \(V^n\) for every integer \(n\ge0\).
proof:
Let K = ℚ_ℓ and let Ω be an algebraic closure of K. Put V_Ω = V ⊗_K Ω, and denote by F also the Ω-linear extension of F to V_Ω; it is again a graded Ω-algebra automorphism. We use the standard characterization: for a finite-dimensional K-vector space W and a K-linear endomorphism T of W, T is semisimple if and only if W_Ω is spanned by eigenvectors of T. For completeness, recall that semisimplicity is equivalent to the minimal polynomial μ_T being squarefree. If μ_T is squarefree, then over Ω it is ∏_{j=1}^s (t-λ_j) with distinct λ_j, and the Chinese remainder theorem gives W_Ω = ⊕_{j=1}^s ker(T-λ_j). Conversely, if W_Ω has an eigenbasis, then the minimal polynomial of T_Ω divides ∏_λ (t-λ) in Ω[t], so μ_T has distinct roots and is squarefree.

For each i, put d_i = deg(s_i) and W_i = span_K{F^m s_i : m ≥ 0}. Since F is a graded automorphism, F^m s_i is homogeneous of degree d_i for every m, so W_i ⊂ V^{d_i}. Also F(W_i) ⊂ W_i, and F|W_i is bijective because F is injective on V and W_i is finite-dimensional. By hypothesis, F|W_i is semisimple. Hence W_i ⊗_K Ω is spanned by eigenvectors of F.

Let E be the Ω-linear span in V_Ω of all eigenvectors of F. We claim that E is an Ω-subalgebra. It contains 1 because F(1)=1. It is closed under addition and scalar multiplication by definition. If x,y ∈ E, write x = Σ_α x_α and y = Σ_β y_β as finite sums of eigenvectors, with F x_α = α x_α and F y_β = β y_β. Then xy = Σ_{α,β} x_α y_β, and each product x_α y_β is either zero or an eigenvector, since F(x_α y_β) = F(x_α)F(y_β) = αβ x_α y_β. Thus xy ∈ E, so E is a subalgebra.

For each i, the element s_i lies in W_i ⊗_K Ω, and W_i ⊗_K Ω is spanned by eigenvectors of F; hence s_i ∈ E. Therefore E contains 1 and all s_i. Since V is generated as a K-algebra by 1,s_1,...,s_r, its scalar extension V_Ω is generated as an Ω-algebra by 1 and the images of the s_i. Hence E = V_Ω.

We next show that E is graded. Let v ∈ E be an eigenvector with F v = λ v, and write v = Σ_n v_n with v_n ∈ V^n ⊗_K Ω. Since F preserves each graded piece, F v_n is the degree-n component of F v = λ v, so F v_n = λ v_n for every n. Thus each nonzero v_n is again an eigenvector, and v is a sum of homogeneous eigenvectors. Consequently E is spanned by homogeneous eigenvectors, so E = ⊕_n (E ∩ (V^n ⊗_K Ω)). Since E = V_Ω, we get E ∩ (V^n ⊗_K Ω) = V^n ⊗_K Ω for every n.

Therefore V^n ⊗_K Ω is spanned by homogeneous eigenvectors of F.
